modules.title: Linux and networking fundamentals
modules.goal: Navigate Linux systems, inspect processes, understand ports, permissions, DNS, and basic troubleshooting.
modules.challenge: Use ps, ss/netstat, dig/nslookup, chmod, system logs, and curl to explain why a service is or is not reachable.
steps: Map the system: print OS, kernel, disk, memory, PATH, and current user.
Investigate a port: list listening sockets and identify the owning process.
Trace a request: resolve a hostname, curl it, and explain each failure mode.
Practice permissions: create a file, change modes, and explain owner/group/other.
Write a mini incident note: symptom, checks, cause, fix, and prevention.
modules.checkpoint: You can explain what is running, what is listening, and why a request succeeds or fails.

quiz.question: Which command is best for checking listening TCP ports? a) chmod b) ss c) mkdir
quiz.explanation: ss shows sockets and listening ports; netstat can work on older systems.

quiz.question: What does exit code 0 usually mean? a) success b) warning c) failure
quiz.explanation: A zero exit code conventionally means the command succeeded.

quiz.question: Which DNS record maps a name to an IPv4 address? a) MX b) A c) TXT
quiz.explanation: A records map names to IPv4 addresses; AAAA records map names to IPv6 addresses.

quiz.question: Which command changes file permissions? a) chmod b) dig c) ps
quiz.explanation: chmod changes permission bits such as read, write, and execute.

modules.title: Git workflows and collaboration
modules.goal: Build safe branching, pull request, rollback, tagging, and release habits.
modules.challenge: Create a feature branch, rebase or merge it cleanly, tag a release, and demonstrate a rollback path.
steps: Create a repo map: branches, remotes, recent commits, and tags.
Run a feature branch mission: two commits, one review-ready diff, one clean merge.
Practice recovery: revert a commit and explain why it is safer than rewriting shared history.
Tag a release and write a tiny changelog.
Draw your team workflow: branch names, PR checks, merge rules, and rollback path.
modules.checkpoint: You can move from change to reviewed commit to release tag to safe rollback.

quiz.question: Which command creates an annotated release marker? a) git tag -a b) git stash c) git fetch
quiz.explanation: Annotated tags are useful for releases because they carry metadata and a message.

quiz.question: Which command safely undoes a committed change by adding a new commit? a) git revert b) git reset --hard c) git clean
quiz.explanation: git revert preserves shared history by creating a new reversing commit.

quiz.question: What is a pull request mainly for? a) code review and merge discussion b) deleting branches c) installing packages
quiz.explanation: Pull requests organize review, discussion, checks, and merging.

quiz.question: Which command downloads remote refs without merging them? a) git fetch b) git commit c) git tag
quiz.explanation: git fetch updates remote-tracking refs while leaving your branch untouched.

modules.title: Shell scripting and automation
modules.goal: Automate repeatable checks with portable Bash scripts and clear exit codes.
modules.challenge: Write a health-check script that validates tools, ports, files, and JSON output with useful failures.
steps: Write a script with strict mode and readable logging.
Validate required commands before doing work.
Parse JSON with jq and fail clearly when data is missing.
Add command-line arguments and a help message.
Test success and failure paths, then capture the expected exit codes.
modules.checkpoint: Your script fails loudly, exits correctly, and helps the next human debug it.

quiz.question: What does set -euo pipefail improve? a) script safety b) color output c) network speed
quiz.explanation: It catches failed commands, unset variables, and pipeline failures earlier.

quiz.question: Which tool is best for JSON parsing in shell scripts? a) jq b) tar c) ssh-keygen
quiz.explanation: jq parses JSON structurally instead of relying on fragile text matching.

quiz.question: Where should error messages usually go? a) stderr b) /dev/null always c) only README files
quiz.explanation: stderr separates errors from normal command output.

quiz.question: Why quote variables like "$file"? a) preserve spaces and avoid glob surprises b) make output green c) install dependencies
quiz.explanation: Quoting prevents word splitting and unintended wildcard expansion.

modules.title: Containers with Docker and Compose
modules.goal: Package an app into an image, run it locally, wire services with Compose, and debug containers.
modules.challenge: Build a small web image, run it with Compose, inspect logs, exec into it, and rebuild after a change.
steps: Build a tiny web image and tag it with a learning version.
Run it locally, inspect logs, exec into the container, and find the served files.
Add Compose so the app starts with one command.
Break one thing on purpose, read the error, and fix it.
Record build, run, debug, and cleanup commands in the lab README.
modules.checkpoint: You can build, run, inspect, break, fix, and clean up a containerized app.
lab_next: Open http://localhost:8080 or run: curl http://localhost:8080
If docker ps still shows devman-web-1, that container came from another Compose project. Stop the root project with: cd ~/devman && docker compose down

quiz.question: Which file usually defines image build steps? a) Dockerfile b) deployment.yaml c) main.tf
quiz.explanation: Dockerfile instructions describe how to build a container image.

quiz.question: What does a container image contain? a) packaged filesystem and metadata b) only source code c) only logs
quiz.explanation: Images bundle filesystem layers plus metadata such as command and environment.

quiz.question: Which command shows container logs? a) docker logs b) git log c) terraform show
quiz.explanation: docker logs reads stdout and stderr captured for a container.

quiz.question: Which command builds an image from the current directory? a) docker build -t name . b) docker ps -a c) docker volume ls
quiz.explanation: docker build reads the Dockerfile and build context.

quiz.question: What does docker compose up do? a) starts services from a Compose file b) creates a Git branch c) applies Terraform state
quiz.explanation: Compose starts multi-container applications from compose.yaml.

quiz.question: Why prefer specific image tags over latest? a) repeatability b) prettier output c) fewer commands
quiz.explanation: Specific tags make builds and deployments easier to reproduce.

modules.title: Kubernetes application operations
modules.goal: Deploy, expose, inspect, scale, and troubleshoot workloads in a local cluster.
modules.challenge: Deploy an app, expose it, scale it, inspect events, roll out a change, and roll it back.
steps: Start a local cluster and confirm kubectl context.
Apply Deployment and Service manifests.
Inspect pods, events, rollout status, and logs.
Scale replicas, restart the rollout, then roll back a bad image tag.
Port-forward the service and write a troubleshooting runbook.
modules.checkpoint: You can deploy, observe, scale, roll out, and recover a local workload.

quiz.question: Which object keeps pods running at a desired replica count? a) Deployment b) Secret c) Namespace
quiz.explanation: Deployments manage ReplicaSets, which keep the desired number of pods running.

quiz.question: Which command shows recent cluster scheduling issues? a) kubectl get events b) docker build c) git tag
quiz.explanation: Events often explain scheduling, image pull, and probe failures.

quiz.question: Which Service type is commonly used for internal-only access? a) ClusterIP b) NodeName c) Dockerfile
quiz.explanation: ClusterIP exposes a service inside the cluster.

quiz.question: What does a readiness probe control? a) whether a pod receives traffic b) Git tag signing c) Docker layer caching
quiz.explanation: Readiness probes tell Kubernetes if the container is ready for service traffic.

modules.title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
modules.goal: Model infrastructure declaratively, review plans, manage state, and structure reusable modules.
modules.challenge: Create local infrastructure, run fmt/validate/plan/apply, inspect state, and destroy safely.
steps: Run init, fmt, validate, and plan before applying anything.
Apply a small local resource and inspect outputs.
Inspect state and explain what Terraform is tracking.
Change an input variable and compare the new plan.
Destroy cleanly and write down the safe workflow order.
modules.checkpoint: You can predict changes with a plan, apply safely, inspect state, and destroy cleanly.

quiz.question: Which command previews infrastructure changes? a) terraform plan b) terraform fmt c) terraform output
quiz.explanation: plan shows proposed changes before apply.

quiz.question: What does Terraform state track? a) managed resource mappings b) shell aliases c) Git branches
quiz.explanation: State maps configuration resources to real infrastructure objects.

quiz.question: Which command formats Terraform files? a) terraform fmt b) terraform destroy c) terraform state rm
quiz.explanation: fmt applies standard Terraform formatting.

quiz.question: Which command initializes providers and backend? a) terraform init b) terraform output c) terraform console only
quiz.explanation: init downloads providers and configures backend state.

modules.title: Configuration automation with Ansible
modules.goal: Write idempotent playbooks, manage inventories, template files, and apply configuration safely.
modules.challenge: Apply a playbook to localhost, prove idempotency, and template a config file from variables.
steps: Create a localhost inventory and run a simple playbook.
Add variables and template or copy a config artifact.
Run the playbook twice and prove idempotency.
Add a handler or conditional task.
Document what changed, what stayed unchanged, and why.
modules.checkpoint: You can run a repeatable playbook and prove the second run is stable.

quiz.question: What does idempotent mean? a) repeated runs converge safely b) every run must fail once c) no variables allowed
quiz.explanation: Idempotent tasks can run repeatedly without unnecessary changes.

quiz.question: Which file lists target hosts? a) inventory b) Dockerfile c) state file
quiz.explanation: Inventories define hosts and groups Ansible should manage.

quiz.question: Which format are playbooks usually written in? a) YAML b) PNG c) ZIP
quiz.explanation: Ansible playbooks are YAML documents.

quiz.question: Why run a playbook twice in a lab? a) prove idempotency b) erase logs c) change branches
quiz.explanation: The second run should usually report no changes for stable tasks.

modules.title: CI/CD pipelines and release automation
modules.goal: Create pipelines that test, scan, build, package, and publish changes with repeatable gates.
modules.challenge: Create a pipeline that runs lint, tests, image build, IaC validation, and artifact publishing steps.
steps: Define pipeline stages: lint, test, build, scan, package, deploy.
Add a minimal workflow file for pull requests and pushes.
Make one check fail, read the log, and fix the cause.
Add an artifact or image build placeholder.
Write promotion rules: what must pass before release.
modules.checkpoint: You can explain every pipeline gate and what evidence it produces.

quiz.question: What is a pipeline gate? a) required check before promotion b) a Kubernetes pod c) a shell prompt
quiz.explanation: Gates prevent bad changes from moving forward.

quiz.question: Which event often triggers CI? a) push or pull request b) disk mount c) DNS lookup
quiz.explanation: CI commonly runs on pushes and pull requests.

quiz.question: What should a deployment pipeline be? a) repeatable and auditable b) manual only c) hidden from logs
quiz.explanation: Repeatability and auditability make releases safer.

quiz.question: Which CI practice protects main branches? a) required passing checks b) committing secrets c) skipping reviews
quiz.explanation: Required checks block merges until validations pass.

modules.title: Logs, metrics, tracing, and alerts
modules.goal: Collect useful signals, query them, and connect alerts to action-oriented runbooks.
modules.challenge: Collect metrics and logs for a sample app, build a minimal dashboard query, and write an alert runbook.
steps: List the signals your sample app should emit: logs, metrics, traces.
Start a local metrics stack or inspect Kubernetes/container logs.
Write three useful queries or log filters.
Draft one alert with impact, owner, and first checks.
Turn the alert into a runbook with recovery and prevention steps.
modules.checkpoint: Your alert points to action, and your runbook helps someone recover calmly.

quiz.question: What are the three common signals? a) logs metrics traces b) tags branches commits c) images layers ports
quiz.explanation: Logs, metrics, and traces are the core observability signals.

quiz.question: What should an alert include? a) action and impact b) only a vague title c) no owner
quiz.explanation: Good alerts tell responders what is wrong and what to do first.

quiz.question: What is a runbook for? a) repeatable incident response b) package installation only c) hiding errors
quiz.explanation: Runbooks guide diagnosis, recovery, and prevention.

quiz.question: Which signal is best for trends and thresholds? a) metrics b) chmod bits c) Git tags
quiz.explanation: Metrics are numeric time series suitable for thresholds and trends.

modules.title: DevSecOps supply chain and runtime security
modules.goal: Add security checks to images, IaC, dependencies, secrets, and cluster policy.
modules.challenge: Find and fix one insecure Dockerfile pattern, one IaC issue, and one secret-handling problem.
steps: Review a Dockerfile for root user, broad permissions, and floating tags.
Scan IaC for risky defaults and missing constraints.
Write a secrets rule: where secrets live and where they never go.
Add one security check to a CI/CD pipeline.
Explain the risk, fix, and verification for each issue you find.
modules.checkpoint: You can name the risk, apply the fix, and verify the control.

quiz.question: Why avoid running containers as root? a) reduces blast radius b) makes images larger c) disables logs
quiz.explanation: A non-root runtime user limits damage if a process is compromised.

quiz.question: Where should secrets not be committed? a) source control b) a secret manager c) environment-specific vault
quiz.explanation: Secrets in Git history are hard to remove and easy to leak.

quiz.question: What is supply chain scanning for? a) dependency and image risk b) changing DNS records c) creating branches
quiz.explanation: Scanning finds vulnerable packages, images, and dependencies.

quiz.question: What is least privilege? a) only needed access b) admin for everyone c) public buckets by default
quiz.explanation: Least privilege gives identities only the permissions they need.

modules.title: Cloud architecture and platform operations
modules.goal: Map DevOps practices to cloud networking, identity, compute, storage, and managed platforms.
modules.challenge: Design a small cloud landing zone with network, identity, compute, storage, and operational guardrails.
steps: Sketch a small environment: network, identity, runtime, storage, monitoring.
Choose one cloud provider and map each component to a managed service.
Define least-privilege roles and tagging rules.
Add backup, cost, and incident-response notes.
Convert the design into an IaC-ready checklist.
modules.checkpoint: Your cloud design has identity, network, cost, backup, and operations guardrails.

quiz.question: What should be tagged for cost control? a) cloud resources b) shell variables only c) Git commits only
quiz.explanation: Tags help allocate, search, and control cloud costs.

quiz.question: What belongs in a landing zone? a) network identity guardrails b) laptop wallpaper c) only app code
quiz.explanation: Landing zones establish foundations such as networking, identity, and policy.

quiz.question: Why separate public and private subnets? a) limit exposure b) speed up Git c) improve font rendering
quiz.explanation: Subnet boundaries help control network access.

quiz.question: What helps prevent surprise bills? a) budgets alerts and tags b) bigger instances c) public access
quiz.explanation: Cost guardrails catch spending changes before they grow.

modules.title: End-to-end DevOps platform capstone
modules.goal: Combine tools into a portfolio-grade workflow from source code to monitored deployment.
modules.challenge: Ship a complete sample service with CI, image build, IaC, Kubernetes deployment, and observability notes.
steps: Pick a tiny service and make it run locally.
Containerize it and document build/run/debug commands.
Deploy it to Kubernetes with health checks.
Add CI validation and release notes.
Finish with architecture notes, runbook, rollback, and next improvements.
modules.checkpoint: Your project tells a complete story from code to deployment to operations.

quiz.question: What makes a capstone strong? a) integrated working workflow b) screenshots only c) no README
quiz.explanation: A strong capstone shows a working path from code to operations.

quiz.question: What should rollback notes describe? a) how to return to a known good version b) how to delete history c) how to ignore alerts
quiz.explanation: Rollback notes should be practical during pressure.

quiz.question: What should the portfolio README explain? a) architecture, commands, tradeoffs b) private secrets c) unrelated tasks
quiz.explanation: A portfolio README should help reviewers understand design and operation.

quiz.question: Why include observability in the capstone? a) operations need signals after deploy b) it makes YAML shorter c) it replaces tests
quiz.explanation: Deployment is not complete until you can observe and respond.
